text.p: Small business owner: if you want to improve your business, change your thinking. Only then you can change your behaviour, your business practices, and finally, your business.
It may not be easy, and professional help isn't cheap. But judging by those who have done it, it certainly can be effective.

Gap International Inc., a Springfield, Pa., management consulting firm whose clients include Fortune 500 companies, offers a business coaching programme for entrepreneurs that teaches what it calls "breakthrough thinking."
This may sound like so much "consult-speak" to the sceptic. But revenue figures cited by participants in Gap courses over the past nine years show "breakthrough" results.

"Our work takes off where motivation ends," said Steve Rosenthal, head of Gap's entrepreneurial unit and developer of its Entrepreneurs' Challenge Course. "Motivation is about people taking certain action. But we found that those actions don't sustain themselves.

"The premise of our work is this: That the thinking that a person brings will shape the actions he or she takes. If you want a person to take actions out of the ordinary -- if you can get at the thinking a person brings, that will shape the actions he takes."
"Breakthrough thinking" isn't needed in certain areas, like choosing a particular accounting programme, Rosenthal said. But things won't happen in other areas without it, he said.

The focus is not on "how to," but rather on all the other elements that make for a successful enterprise -- the firm's way of doing business, how the entrepreneur connects with employees and customers, his or her personal performance and how all those elements affect the business' results.

"It's scary, trying to start a new business," said Rosenthal. "Technical training does not equip people to have the confidence that they will be successful in the world of business. The 'how to' doesn't deal with the confidence issue, which is something we found is common to all businesses."
Entrepreneurs who have done Gap's programme say it was instrumental in helping them expand their businesses and boost revenues.
Claire Sullivan, who started a corporate event planning company in Houston in 1989 and did the Gap programme in 1993, says it had "definite, measurable results" for her.

"When I started the course I was at $190,000 in sales annually and doubled my sales in 1994 to just under $400,000," she said. The following year she went to $600,000 in revenues and is now on the way to $1 million.
"It is very results-oriented. You commit to what your goals are each month, and the coaching that they provide really makes you stay on track," Sullivan said of the programme.

"As an independent business owner, I have no one to report to. This is one way for me to constantly be held accountable. I can't imagine not having this group of people and this coaching. I continue to get more productive and to look at bigger things."
Drew Hannah, general manager of Cambridge, Mass., software maker Softbridge Inc., did the Gap programme prior to joining the firm, which had not ever been profitable in its 11 years.
"The people I joined pretty much expected to continue to lose money every quarter," he said. "I looked at it and said 'This is nuts. We should be making money.'"

Hannah said one of the toughest challenges was setting a personal goal of making a profit and getting his management team to see that it was possible. "Part of the training we get in Gap is how to go beyond what you planned and set a goal that's much higher, mostly for the sake of stretching oneself and developing other possibilities," he said.

"It's about being in that space outside of your comfort zone and being willing to set a goal way outside of where you're comfortable, and yet being willing and able to make a commitment to do that anyway so you can see what happens. Then you have to let people know that you're committed to it."

Hannah did just that after joining Softbridge three years ago. "Two quarters later we became profitable and have stayed profitable since then," he said. "Now the same team sees itself as part of a team that stays profitable every quarter."

Bryan Hoffman, who owns a Philadelphia landscape architecture firm, did Gap's course in 1994-95 after launching his business three years earlier. "We were doing great, but it seemed to me that it was just happening around me, and I wasn't really doing anything to make it happen," he said.
"I really wasn't driving it. I saw the course as an opportunity to take the business and myself to the next level," he said.

After completing the programme, Hoffman transferred the leadership from himself to a management team. "It's allowed people in my organisation to really grow into positions that are much bigger. It's the only way that the growth could occur -- it was too much for me to handle. I didn't see that before I went into the course."

Hoffman later sent his office manager to the course. "I saw a lot of things change for her," he said. "She's not a business owner, so it's different, but it was definitely worth my investment to put her in the course.
"She's taken on things in the company that she never would have imagined she would. She took on creating a new product line -- she launched it, and it did $25,000 in revenues last year."

Gap's Entrepreneurs' Challenge Course is currently offered in Boston, Chicago, Philadelphia, Washington and Houston, with classes limited to 20 participants. It costs $9,200 for 12 four-hour sessions spread over of six to nine months, along with personal coaching on current business situations.
For more information, check out Gap's web site at GapInter.com. or call 610-328-0308.
